blocks.content: Durability means one thing: once the database says "committed", that data survives anything power cut, crash, OS kernel panic. The database must never lose a committed transaction.
The core problem: RAM is fast but volatile. Disk is slow but permanent. The challenge is making writes permanent without making them unbearably slow.
1. The problem: RAM vs disk

Data written to RAM is gone the moment the power dies. But writing every change directly to disk on every operation is too slow a random disk write takes ~10ms. At 1000 transactions/second, that's the bottleneck.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399130610-121719041.png
The insight: sequential disk writes are fast much faster than random writes. Appending to the end of a log file is sequential. This is the foundation of everything.
2. The Write-Ahead Log (WAL)
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396519048-806280806.png
blocks.alt: A transaction writes to the WAL sequentially before commit, then fsync forces it to disk as the real durability point, only then is COMMIT acknowledged, while actual table pages get flushed later by a background checkpoint

items: Transaction runs in memory (buffer pool)→ very fast, but not yet saved to disk
Before commit, all changes are written toWAL (log file on disk)→ done as a fast sequential write
Thenfsync()is called → forces data to be physically written to disk→ this is the real durability point
Only after this, database sends COMMIT→ now data is guaranteed safe
Actual table data (pages) are written later by a background checkpoint process→ safe because WAL already has everything

blocks.content: 3. Crash recovery ( WAL replay )
If the database crashes, the WAL is what saves you. On restart, the database replays the WAL forward to reconstruct everything that was committed but not yet flushed to data pages.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399130610-251205854.png
When a crash happens before the WAL is written, the transaction exists only in memory and has not been saved anywhere on disk. Since the WAL was never written, there is no record of that transaction.
After restart, the database simply ignores it as if it never happened. The client may see an error, but the database remains safe because no partial or incorrect data was stored.
When a crash happens after the WAL is written and fsync is completed, the situation is different. Even if the actual data pages were not written yet, the WAL already contains all the changes.
On restart, the database reads the WAL and replays those changes to rebuild the data. This ensures that all committed transactions are fully recovered and no data is lost.
The WAL is an append-only journal of every change. Even if all in-memory pages are lost, replaying the WAL from the last checkpoint forward recovers every committed transaction perfectly.
4. WAL also powers replication

The same WAL that provides crash safety is also streamed to replica servers in real time. Each replica replays the same log and becomes an exact copy of the primary. Durability and scaling come from the same mechanism.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399130610-26201767.png
The primary database writes all changes to the WAL. This same WAL is sent to replica servers. Each replica replays the WAL to apply the exact same changes, so they stay in sync with the primary.
Because all replicas use the same WAL, they maintain an identical copy of the data. If the primary database fails, a replica can take over immediately without losing any data.
